title: Connection Pooling
explain: When one request fans out to many downstream services, opening a fresh TCP and TLS connection per call wastes round trips, and an outbound host only has so many ports and sockets. I keep an independent connection pool per downstream host with a maximum size and idle reuse. The cap is both a quota that protects the downstream and a cache of warm connections.
model:
The problem (user's framing): outbound TCP slots are limited; with huge fan-out (1M connections) it cannot work naively.

```
                    +--> [Pool for Service-A]  max 500 --> Service-A
[Fanout task] ------+--> [Pool for Service-B]  max 500 --> Service-B
                    +--> [Pool for Service-C]  max 500 --> Service-C
```

Wrong approach 1, **one global pool** (first grabber wins):

1. **Deadlock.** A request needing A, B and C holds A and B and waits for C, which others hold while waiting for A or B.
2. **Connections are not interchangeable.** A socket is bound to its 4-tuple; a connection to A can never carry a request to B.
3. **Noisy neighbour.** One caller takes 50,000 slots and flattens a downstream.

Wrong approach 2, **a per-host counter with no pool**: caps concurrency but throws connections away, so every request redoes the TCP/TLS handshake.

Right: **pool per host/endpoint**, with `max size`, idle reuse and idle timeout (`requests.Session` with `HTTPAdapter(pool_maxsize=50)`, Go `MaxIdleConnsPerHost`). Layer a [rate limiter](#/sd/f/rate-limiter) and [circuit breaker](#/sd/f/circuit-breaker) on top.

Pooling is transport layer (L4); authn/authz happen per request at L7, so reuse skips neither. See [TCP connection](#/sd/f/tcp-connection).

details.q: A global pool has 100 slots, and 100 fanout requests each take one for Service-A and now each needs a slot for Service-B. What happens?
details.a: Deadlock: every slot is held by a request waiting for another slot, so none can finish. Per-host pools cannot deadlock this way, since the A slots and B slots are separate.

details.q: Why can't warm connections to A be lent to calls to B?
details.a: A TCP connection is bound to one remote IP and port (the four-tuple), so a socket to A can only talk to A. Pools must be per destination.

details.q: 2,000 req/s at a mean 50 ms over HTTP/1.1. How many connections are busy?
details.a: 100 on average: 2,000 x 0.05 s (Little's law). Size the pool above that with headroom for bursts, and remember HTTP/2 multiplexing lets one connection carry many requests.

details.q: RTT is 40 ms. How much does reusing an idle pooled connection save per request?
details.a: A fresh connection costs a TCP handshake (1 RTT) and a TLS 1.3 handshake (1 RTT) before the request itself, so reuse saves 2 RTT, 80 ms. At high request rates that is also a lot of ephemeral ports and CPU.

details.q: A client caps itself at 100 in-flight calls per host with a semaphore but opens and closes a connection per call. What is still wrong?
details.a: Every call pays the handshake and burns ephemeral ports (connections linger in TIME_WAIT). A pool reuses idle connections; the semaphore only gives the quota half.

details.q: Will an upstream mind lots of idle pooled connections or reject unauthenticated ones?
details.a: Not at the TCP layer: the handshake is independent of authn/authz, which happen per request. But idle connections cost the server file descriptors and memory, so size pools modestly and let idle ones time out.

prompts.q: Why is a pool per downstream host better than one global pool? Give three reasons.
points: Global pool can deadlock when requests need several hosts
A socket is bound to one remote host so connections are not interchangeable
A greedy caller can take all slots and overload a downstream
Per-host max is a quota and isolates failures
Reuse of warm connections avoids repeated handshakes

prompts.q: Walk through what happens on the first and second request to the same host with a Session.
points: First: pool empty, open connection, keep it in the pool afterwards
Second: take the idle socket, write the request directly
Concurrent callers share a bounded pool and wait or fail when it is exhausted

prompts.q: Size and protect the pools for a fanout service with a thousand downstreams.
points: Busy connections equal rate times latency
Per-host max, plus a cap on the number of hosts pooled
Rate limit and circuit breaker per host
